whisper.text:
Profiles in Holography is brought to you through the generous support of the International Holography Fund. For more information, visit their website at holographyfund.org. Hello everyone, this is Frank DeFreitas and I would like to welcome you to another installment of HoloTalk. My guest for this broadcast is Stephen Smith of Lasersmith. Now the show is a little bit over 30 minutes long, so instead of me giving you the introduction, I'm going to take you over there and let Steve do it for himself. He gives a wonderful description of his past history in holography and his thoughts about holography in general and the future. So without further ado, here's Stephen Smith on HoloTalk. Good afternoon, Stephen speaking. Hello Stephen, how are you? It's Frank DeFreitas. Hello Frank, how are you? Doing good. I want to welcome you to the show. I've always wanted to speak to you, but I've never had the opportunity for the two of us to meet. I know you have a rich history in holography. You also have the luckiest name in holography. I can't think of any other name that would go after laser that would fit as well as Lasersmith. You know, I have to give a really good friend of mine from the early days I was in Chicago back in the early 70s with coming up with that name because I was running around with some holograms and my middle initial. And it was Al and he just started saying, oh, it's that Lasersmith guy. Oh. And that was kind of funny. It was really, so it was like a no-brainer after what started out as a snide remark ended up being something I'm quite proud to play around with. But you know why I really liked it too? Because of the village Smithy. He was, or she was, you know, I look at this thing in history, that artisan in the village that made stuff. Yes, exactly. And for me, that was something. I didn't know much what holography was about. You, in those early days, you were like taking these materials and trying to smith them into a hologram. Tool them as it be. But at any rate, yeah. Why don't you start off by telling the listeners a little bit about your early history. And I imagine that was in the Chicago area? Well, yeah, let's look at it that way. I got my Bachelor of Science degree from Southern Illinois University in Carbondale. And in between my junior year and my senior year, I took a year off, what I thought was going to be a year off, went up to Chicago and worked, got a job in the photo industry doing a lot of photo compose, the kind of photography work that you did at advertising agencies. Oh, I see. Yeah, like pre-press color separating things. Color separation? Yes. Where you're doing what would be considered posterized color? Yes. You know, doing a lot of work with different codoliths so you can, you know, comp pictures inside of other pictures. Okay. So this turned out to be really fundamentally helpful a few years later. I went back, I saw my first hologram at a School of the Art Institute media and new technology show that was a number of grad students had put together. And believe it or not, there was a hologram in there from Dr. Jiang. Oh, what year was that? This was... It was like something like 76. And this is a hologram that was a little car. I think it was called Quick Turnaround. Okay. And it was a little circular hologram. Oh, that was one of his first 360 laser transmission cylinder holograms. Yeah. And I was very captured by that. At that point in my career, I was really kind of a fine art photographer. I had a 4x5 view camera. I used to spend my off days... Slept around Chicago doing black and white and color work. I had my own dye transfer lab in one of my bedrooms in my apartment. And I was doing color separations and doing... If your listeners are familiar with a photographer by the name of George Tice, it's kind of like urban landscape photography. Okay. And that's what I was doing in 75 and 74. And then I saw this hologram. And as an image maker in photography, I was very much about a printmaker. I really... Cared a lot about the quality of the print. That was a part of the process that communicated my vision or image through to the viewer. And I was very much an art photographer. And so I called my old instructor, Chuck Swedland, down at Southern Illinois. And I said, you know, I want to come back and finish up my senior year. And I've caught wind of this new thing called holography. And I want to know if you might let me spin that up into my... And I said, okay. And he said, okay. And I said, okay.

Zitter, who was over in the physics department. That's interesting. And Dr. Zitter had a helium neon laser. So they said, you know what, we can make this work. Come on back. So I went back down in 78, 77, 78 to finish my senior year and did kind of a mix of holography and photography. And I need to put something in here real important. After I saw my first hologram and found out that it was made by a physics professor up in Lake Forest, just north of Chicago, I went and signed up for his summer holography workshops. Oh, okay. And took two of them. And that really, it was like people were getting frustrated with me because all I ever talked about was holography and trying to get a laser. You were called to do this. It was just, yeah, it's like that little mouse or little squirrel that sees a shiny thing, needs to collect it. Something happened. I was just, I have to know how to do this. To me, it was an extension of the image. Now it was the ultimate printmaking. I wasn't dealing with dyes or silver anymore on a paper. I was able to make structures that diffracted light. So the color in my photographs could be light. That's what appealed to me. That's what got my dander up, as they say. And where did you go after that? Well, I came back and again, went back to work at the same company. They were actually kind of pleased that I came back in. I had a place called Gamma Photo and I had the job of the manager of the duplication department, which was like an extension of the stuff I'd been doing. But then I started pestering them. I started showing them my holograms that I was making. And I own a little five milliwatt laser. And at the time, when I moved back, I moved down into the western section of the Chicago Loop. That's where the old vegetable markets used to be near Fulton Street. I had a loft photography studio. I was still doing photography on the side, but I had to support myself. So I had a full-time job as the manager of this colored dupe department. And I'd bring them in my holograms and I'd show them and I'd say, you know, these are really, really getting kind of interesting to do. What do you think? And they kind of were like, you know, we're, we don't see this being interesting. Isn't that something? And they got, I got in trouble with the management. So I, at that point, was interested in doing holography full time and was trying to figure out a way to do it. And I was like, well, I'm going to do it. So I looked for another, another photo lab where they had an opening on the night shift so I could work from five in the evening until one in the morning. And then I had days to work in my little lab and took that job over at K&S Photographics. So now we're talking 79. And in the same time was, had built up my little lab, was doing holograms with a little 2.5 or 5 milliwatt Heaney. That was a major investment back then, a 5 milliwatt Heaney. That they were doing. Yeah. Yeah. That was like serious money. It was like more than $2,000. It certainly was. And, and it was like, and it was such a pitiful amount of light. And I was making little tiny, like one inch in diameter and reflection holograms that you could like barely see because nobody had really heard about pyrochrome yet. Okay. So we were doing all this, you know, really heavily silver laden holograms that were fixed. And because of the, you know, they shot in red, but there was all the silver in them and collapsing. And so they were green. You were probably working with, you know, with the mature chloride and some of those other chemicals. Yeah. Yeah. Good stuff. Bad news. And here's where the nice note, another little fun caveat happens. I'm going to have a lot of friends in my building that are students at the school of the art Institute. And I'm going to all the weekends, going to parties at different students' house. And I'm at a party one evening and I'm talking to a woman who's there, a girl, trying to make conversation. And at one point she just got frustrated and said, you know, there's another guy here who's trying to talk to me about the same stuff. This is holography stuff. I'm going to introduce you to him. You want to talk to somebody about this? Go talk to him. And she introduced me to Tom Svetkovich. Oh, yes. And so in meeting Tom, I found out there was somebody else that was like really keenly interested in holography and he was doing some consulting with Zenith. So that kind of spun. So in the summers, I'm doing like workshops and holography at Lake Forest. In the daytime, Tom and I are kind of talking about how can we make holograms work. Yeah. Yeah. And we started, we figured, well, one thing we can do is this is obviously more money than either one of us have. Why don't we try to do this thing? There was a young man, a guy in Chicago who had started a thing called a cooperative dark room where people could rent time on enlargers who didn't, you know, have a dark room. I thought, why couldn't we do something like that for holography? Why don't we have like a cooperative holography lab? And that began the Chicago Holographic Cooperative. Oh, I never, I have never heard of that. So connections, myself, Tom, some students, people, Victor Heredia, Rick Bruck, Melissa Crenshaw, a whole group of people that have been taking holography classes up at Lake Forest and also at the 1134 Gallery of Holography in Washington.

Rick Bruck, Melissa Crenshaw, a whole group of people that had been taking holography classes up at Lake Forest and also at the 1134 Gallery of Holography in Washington Street in Chicago, were all actually kind of milling around Chicago looking for, like, how can we do this? So we started meeting at my studio at 952 West Lake Street. It was a photography studio. And they had my little holography lab there that really wasn't much, but I was able to do some things. And we would have monthly meetings. What are you doing? Bring in holograms. Talk about holograms. Who wants to start a lab? You know, Tom had a laser, had some equipment. And we ended up meeting a woman that owned an old firehouse a couple blocks from me at 114 North Aberdeen. And she was like, I've got a tenant on the first floor. He's got a meatpacking company. Get these trucks with smelly meat in there. I'll be glad to rent you the first floor. Do whatever you want. So Tom and I took off. We got a lease. One-year lease. Took the back of it up to start with and built our first table. Wow. Started putting the table together. Now we're talking this late 79 and going into the spring of 1980. And we had the first table up. The darkroom processing was happening. And he and I had built, had been making, you know, he had a bigger laser. Yay. Red laser? Yep. And there we were. We were making four by five holograms. Yeah. I think that's right around the time of the first workshop, the symposium on holography. Okay. That would be 82. Okay. So right around 82, paper by Lon Moore. Color control. Oh, yes. And holography. Yes. Tom and I were like, oh, this is going to be hot. Right away, ran back to the lab. Started playing around with processing and the color control, which is P-benzoquinone, which is another really bad leach you didn't really want to be messing with. Anything comes in a package. It's a cardboard box. Inside of that is a aluminum foil cellophane bag that's been vacuum sealed, which inside of that is another glass container. Inside of that is another container. It's like in a skull and crossbones on the front. So P-benzoquinone from the holographer. That was to do your pseudo-color holograms, right? That's when we started doing pseudo-color holograms. And up at that point, we were meeting every day at the little holography lab in the back of this firehouse, making holograms, some single color, some transmission, trying to put together what would be the equivalent of a portfolio. I knew some art directors at a number of different agencies around Chicago. I had a couple of really good friends who were also photographers that were doing commercial photography work, and they were putting me in touch with people. And we put together three color control holograms and went into an advertising agency that was called Franklin Company. What holograms were they? There was two holograms of little shells I had found on the beach of crabs. Okay. So there was a crab shell that was green and a crab shell that was gold, floating through the surface of the plate. And we met with a guy, an art director, whose name was Bill Takazuki. And at the time, he had a big client called McDonald's, and they were doing point-of-sale signage for McDonald's. He said, you know what? This is, like, really, really cool stuff. He said, if you had more equipment, could you make these bigger and could you do these better? Because he said, because nobody's ever come in here and showed me holograms that could be, this is that color and this is that color. So Tom and I came back. We set up their little exhibition room with the 12 different holograms. Two were laser-lit. A couple were, we even had built a case. The case was, like, took two people to carry it up, all made out of wood. All the little slots for the holograms were set in, the laser just set in. Wow. The whole thing. Set it up. They brought in a number of different account execs. It was there for about a four-hour period. We hung around and answered questions while people were there. Then a guy came there who was the account exec for McDonald's, and he said, we're going to have a meeting. Leave all this stuff here. I want you here tomorrow morning at 9 o'clock. Came in the next morning at 9, met the head buyer from the McDonald's Corporation. Spent all day at the agency talking about ideas. At the end of that day, we walked out with a contract to do, a holographic art piece for McDonald's new school campus. Wow. That was in Oak Brook. It wasn't a lot of money. He said, look, we can't bankroll you, but if you do stuff for us and we build a program, we'll make this happen. That was a happy day. Huh? That was a happy day. That was a day. That was the day we called up Coherent and convinced them that they needed to sell us a 5-watt Krypton laser. Which was interesting. That's the whole story itself. It was self-convincing. It's like, you guys are who? And you're going to do what? Yes. But they did. Well, wasn't that nice? So we did. And that's what I went that very next day to my job and said, you know, you're right. I've got to do this holography thing.

Nice. So we did, and that's what, I went that very next day to my job and said, you know, you're right. I've got to do this holography thing. So I went full time. And from that day forward, there was never a day we were not busy doing holograms for something. Wow, isn't that something? And you have a number of patents to your name as well. Through the work that developed with, you know, such a thread. Because a lot of early work was reflection holograms. And then we got involved in doing photoresist. And photoresist led to mass replication. And mass replication led to baseball cards. And baseball cards led to the multiple camera system. Are you involved with security holograms as well? Well, we were for a while. For a while. But you have to, in realizing that. That part of my thread that was the photographer, I was very much interested in holography as that next step forward in image making. You know, and that's a big open canvas to paint on. It could be still work. It could be, you know, that hybrid between video and still. I mean, that's what holography is so phenomenal. It's really a four-dimensional tool in many ways. What does holography do that gives us the ability to say that it's the next step? In imaging. What is that next step? I feel it still has not given us its full potential. It has not, through many of the reasons are hardware related. You know, resolution, coming up with devices that can have the resolution you need for holographic imaging. But it's getting there. Real-time, updatable 3D displays. I mean, if there was one thing that a hologram can do that. Other types of stereoscopic media cannot do. And that is a correctly rendered three-dimensional scene where convergence and focus are correct. And that to me, and then when you tie to that renewable at whatever, 60 frames a second, it becomes that phenomenal visual interface. I mean, our eyes are the most developed tool set of our whole body. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. I wasn't there myself, but I remember seeing a photo of you with a long bank of individual cameras so that you could do portraiture without having any amount of time pass. It would just be one exposure on multiple cameras. Was that you? Yes. What's the story? Did you follow through with that? I did a lot of work with that for a while. That was the 36-camera multi-camera system. The impetus for doing that was having done what was the equivalent of still life photography, objects on a table lit. We were beginning to bump our heads against the boundary of, could you do something that's a real thing? We already had a really good contract going with Upper Deck. Smith and Svetkovich holography had ended. Tom and I had split. We had different directions. The Lasersmith came into being. Within that period of time of the Lasersmith, we got heavily involved in trying to break that other boundary, get holography able to deliver to whoever was interested in it, besides the artist and the commercial side, images of the kind of things they could go to a photographer and get in real life. This became kind of an outlandish idea in one sense. Sure, I've got a really rich photography history. I know about Muybridge. Multiple camera system, imaging sequences of images to kind of like dissect motion. There had been people that had built multiple camera systems to do stereo photography. Nobody had ever taken the challenge with the new cameras, the available electronic shutter control that was now available, and specifically to deal with them relative to the holographic image problem. Sitting down and doing a quick calculation, I worked out basically if I took the 7 to 9 millimeters that you might consider to be that active area behind your pupil that your retina is at when you're looking at something at M's length, how many different views do I need to have to kind of fill that out 15 inches wide? That's where the number 36 came from. Oh, I see. So, put together a small group of it. Lasersmith was half of the funds. Gary Zucker, who was the marketing, the marketing guy who put together the Upper Deck deal, put together another quarter, and Dr. Jung also coupled in, and we formed a group called Advanced Holographic Imaging Technology, AHIT. AHIT.

another quarter, and Dr. Jung also coupled in. And we formed a group called Advanced Holographic Imaging Technology, AHIT. And that was specifically to do image capture initially for sports cards for Upper Deck. I see. I want to ask you about Upper Deck. The first shot we did was the ballerina. Yes, I know that piece. Really big success with the little galleries. Yes, very nice. Yes. The Upper Deck, there's people that still ask questions about the Upper Deck, and maybe you can sort of clarify a few things on that. The footage that someone sees in one of the Upper Deck cards that provides the several seconds of action. Yes, but you've got to be careful which ones, because there is a group of them that I did with this camera system, and then there are later ones that were done, which would just be like a... very high number of multi-channel holograms. It had nothing stereo to do about it. So there's... I see. I want to be real clear. There's later holograms that have been done for Upper Deck that have got nothing to do with the multiple camera system. Okay. They're just taking, you know, 25 or 30 frames of video footage and imaging them sequentially like you would in a stereogram, except they don't have any three-dimensional data. Yes. And they'll do some tracking, because they've got to get rid of any camera jitter or blur. They might even, you know, stay... relatively positioned with the carrier of the ball or the guy hitting the... you know, whatever. Mm-hmm. But that's different. That's not the multiple camera system. Yes. There was only one set of hockey cards done with the multiple camera system. Okay. So Mark Mathia, Brett Hall, one other really great hockey guy. Were they more or less static images? No, they were... They were motions, like a smile. This is where there was the interesting problem. This is where I was kind of pushing the envelope too much. These have motion. I've got one. Okay. Okay. Okay. This is where Mark Mathia and Brett Hall are fighting for the puck. Oh. So as you move the hologram back and forth, not only are they 3D and skating at you, but their sticks are also going back and forth. I see. I've got another one where I'm trying to remember, and I'm sitting here grasping for the guy's name. He was from Canada originally, but he was a big, big-name player for the California-Los Angeles team. I can't remember his name. But he does what he really... He smacks the puck, and it's... It's reminiscent of that strobe photograph of the guy swinging the tennis racket and hitting the ball. Okay. In the sense that every single sectional sweep of the hockey stick, up to the point where it hits the puck and the puck speeds away, is there, but it's there three-dimensionally as well as sequentially. Okay. That's interesting, because there were a few of us trying to determine whether we were actually seeing any dimensional change. There were dimensional properties to some of those cards that were produced for a national chain. I think it was Denny's or something. Right. All of that's... You know, I did a bunch of those for American Banknote, but they were not done with the multiple camera system. I was hired as a... But there is dimensional property to that, or are we all mistaken? But those were... Resake, because I think I overspoke on top of what you're saying. I'm sorry. Those cars that we're speaking of that you said were... produced with American Banknote, but not with the multiple camera system. Are we correct in seeing dimensional properties to those cards? They're not. I would say you're just kind of visually thinking you're seeing it. Thinking we're seeing it. Okay. It's a single camera and it's a sequence of time. Yeah. Because we were with them... The person ran by or hit... Some of them were baseball. Yeah. We were with Ken Dunkley, who was an early holographer. I know him. Yes. And he has a system where you can see three-dimensional from one perspective. I don't know if you've ever seen his system or not. It has to do with a small pinhole and iris viewer that you use just with magazine photos. And the photos wind up being almost like the old Viewmaster images. They completely go 3D. But you're just looking... Check that out sometime. It's amazing. You ever can send me a link if there's any... Yes, I will. I will do that. It really makes your hair stand up on edge. It's something to see. So I was wondering if the same type of thing might have been happening with those cards because we passed a few of those around over the summer. And some of us said there is most definitely dimension going on here. And everybody was saying, well, how could there be? It's only one perspective. But if there... Let's say if the motion that's been captured... I became really aware of this with a multiple camera system. I had to make sure that people moved, spun, or directed their motion, in particular directions. If they moved counterclockwise, which was... The cameras triggered from left to right. Because I kind of thought, like, you know, not, you know, like being kind of Western...

was the cameras triggered from left to right. Because I kind of thought, not like being kind of Western, reading English, learning style, we read from left to right. So my holograms are made to go left to right. You tip them from the left to the right. So your right eye is always advanced in time from your left eye. If a person moves the wrong direction, if they move right to left, so they're keeping position with the tracking of the cameras, there's no stereoscopic correct data. And so they become flattened, or if they move too fast, they actually invert. So I have an image of a peacock dancer where her hand moves the wrong way, and it looks like it's going back through her back. The same thing could be said of these motion images. If there is some motion, and it's the motion sequentially, they are also recorded in time left to right. So at the latter time, if the baseball player, let's say, he's hitting the ball, and sequentially the bat has come around, so you're seeing the bat to the right, and the right eye, but it's to the left in the left eye because it hadn't quite gotten to that position, you're going to perceive that as being stereoscopic data. I see. His body will look 2D because it didn't move much, or it might have rotated the same way, and it might look a little bit 3D. Yes. But that's how I think you're getting those. They'd be like false depth. Wonderful. I believe that would explain things, and we'll have to take a second look at them and take note to what we see as we move them back and forth, rotate them in opposite directions, and see if that dimensional effect disappears depending on which way we turn it. Yes. Yeah, I think that's worth looking at. Yeah. I'll take it. And do forward me his little pinhole 3D. Definitely anything 3D. I'm getting very interested in 3D again. It kind of evolved away from it after having left the Media Lab. Mm-hmm. I will have to check around here because I had one of his units, and I think I may know where it's at because I loaned it to somebody. They did send it back to me, and I put it in storage. I will get that out. And if you forward to me your address, I'll send you one of the units to take a look at and try out. Oh, I'll be glad to do that. I think you would enjoy that. And I hope it works for you. It doesn't work for everyone. The person I sent it to said he could not get three dimension from it. I did, immediately. And I swear, the hair on my arms stood up straight. It was just bizarre. Because there's no dimensional information. It's a photograph, and a magazine. But if you're looking at... I mean, the mountains are off in the distance. The trees come towards you. You'll see. Maybe it'll work for you. Definitely, I'll have to look at this. Okay. So what are your plans for the future now? I imagine that... Oh, I don't know what your age is, but I guess you have to be thinking about retirement sometime in the future. Who thinks of retirement? Come on. But before that, what would you like to do and still achieve? Well, I'm seeing things... I think it's very interesting, again, in this kind of hybrid area of digital holography. And having worked with Steve Benton the seven years I was at the... almost eight years at the Media Lab, and some of the side work... I mean, mostly my work was with the holographic printer and autostereoscopic displays, but I, from time to time, would get involved in the rendering hardware side of the holovideo system. And real-time holographic displays are an interesting thing. It's an interesting phenomenon. And with the work that I did in the one-step printer and the renderer and the type of holographic pixels that we devised and imaged, I can see a direct correlation to a real-time holographic display and feature sizes of some of these devices are starting to get down to... Like, example, there's a spaceflight modulator that's got 9-5 micron feature sizes on. Yes. And you can get that in a phase-only mode that gives you 2 pi. Per cell rotation. So that actually starts to get pretty interesting. Lost me on that one, but that's okay. But it's a phase thing. In other words, you can get enough phase. Think about it. Why do we do holographic lasers? Because we can't record the phase of light. Yes. We can record its color. We can record its brightness. But we can't record which direction it's going. So holography has been stuck forever with lasers because that's the only way we've come up to record the phase of light. But all light actually does have phase. Maybe that's a new research direction. How to record the phase of light. In most cases, it's just random phase. Is that correct? Well, it's random, but it is coming from somewhere. Yes. So it can be controlled. I mean, there is spatial information in that beam of light.

In most cases, it's just random phase. Is that correct? Well, it's random, but it is coming from somewhere. Yes. So it can be controlled. I mean, there is spatial information in that beam of light that's bouncing off that switch to my left. But so, you know, there's some interesting directions. And I think right now what's going on with some of the real-time 3D displays that are diffractive in nature, the University of Arizona work that's going on with those photorefractive polymers that can be written to, that's pretty exciting. Like I said, these little, right now they're 1024 by 1024, but they have 5 micron feature sizes. And if you are willing to pay them enough, they'll give you one that's phase only. That's looking pretty interesting. So I think there's maybe a path to a real-time holographic display. That would be wonderful because there's so many competing technologies now. There are. The holography is really taking a back seat, too. We have to work a little harder maybe to get something out of it. But, you know. You know, there's, what's that group that's doing that thing where they're, you know. Do you remember a few years back there was a woman from Stanford that had done a little doped cube, a little crystal? Oh, yes. She was scanning an infrared laser into it. Yes. And basically drawing, you know, X and Y scanning into it and getting fluorescence off of the molecules. Big kid out at SPIE. Yes, I remember that. At Atonix West a few years back. There were lines almost reminiscent of one. Emmett Leaf had his holograms at the Optical Society of America. But there's a group now, and I will have to. I apologize for not having this. I just came across their website yesterday. And they, optics. Gosh darn it, where is it now? But they took that same idea. You've got a little cube. It's two centimeters by ten, two centimeters. But it's kind of like filled with little particles that will fluoresce with infrared illumination. So they're, you know, X and Y scanning. You know, they're doing a little bit of what, like. Mike Halley was doing at the Media Lab, which was kind of like doing real-time rendering with slices. So you kind of couple that together, and you have this little two-centimeter cube. And if you give me one second, I'm actually dialing through my e-mails, and I will tell you the name of this company. That's pretty exciting, although it's not holographic. It's interesting. It's a hybrid thing, right? Yeah, it's another competing technology. Because it's a scanner and getting three-dimensional fluorescing to go on. So that's not holographic in that sense. But they'll call it a holographic. Yes. They'll call it a hologram anyway. They will. Thank you, CNN. Yes. I get so frustrated when non-holography gets mistagged. Yeah. It's very unfortunate, but it happens every day. And it's having an adverse effect on holographic workshops and holographic exhibits. Because I've had the public come to shows where they would look at the holograms on the wall, and they would turn around and say, this is not what I expected a hologram to be. This is ridiculous. It's really a good observation. Because, you know, Star Wars, which was great in so many ways, Princess Leia was the bane of holography for a long time. Because you would get calls. Well, that's what we want. What do you mean you can't do that? Lucas can do that. And the same thing has happened with this. And again, what's really too bad is why don't they just call it what it was? Because it really was good for what it was. It's kind of like tracking, you know, motion capture for blue screen. Motion rendering. Or multiple view capture for blue screen. That's all they were doing. Oh, 3D icon. Okay. They have a thing called C-space. Okay. But see, they're being honest. Profiles in Holography is brought to you through the generous support of the International Holography Fund. For more information, visit their website at holographyfund.org. Hello everyone, this is Frank DeFreitas and I would like to welcome you to another installment of HoloTalk. My guest for this broadcast is Stephen Smith of Lasersmith. Now the show is a little bit over 30 minutes long, so instead of me giving you the introduction, I'm going to take you over there and let Steve do it for himself. He gives a wonderful description of his past history in holography and his thoughts about holography in general and the future. So without further ado, here's Stephen Smith on HoloTalk. Good afternoon, Stephen speaking. Hello Stephen, how are you? It's Frank DeFreitas. Hello Frank, how are you? Doing good. I want to welcome you to the show. I've always wanted to speak to you, but I've never had the opportunity for the two of us to meet. I know you have a rich history in holography. You also have the luckiest name in holography. I can't think of any other name that would go after laser that would fit as well as Lasersmith. You know, I have to give a really good friend of mine from the early days I was in Chicago back in the early 70s with coming up with that name because I was running around with some holograms and my middle initial. And it was Al and he just started saying, oh, it's that Lasersmith guy. Oh. And that was kind of funny. It was really, so it was like a no-brainer after what started out as a snide remark ended up being something I'm quite proud to play around with. But you know why I really liked it too? Because of the village Smithy. He was, or she was, you know, I look at this thing in history, that artisan in the village that made stuff. Yes, exactly. And for me, that was something. I didn't know much what holography was about. You, in those early days, you were like taking these materials and trying to smith them into a hologram. Tool them as it be. But at any rate, yeah. Why don't you start off by telling the listeners a little bit about your early history. And I imagine that was in the Chicago area? Well, yeah, let's look at it that way. I got my Bachelor of Science degree from Southern Illinois University in Carbondale. And in between my junior year and my senior year, I took a year off, what I thought was going to be a year off, went up to Chicago and worked, got a job in the photo industry doing a lot of photo compose, the kind of photography work that you did at advertising agencies. Oh, I see. Yeah, like pre-press color separating things. Color separation? Yes. Where you're doing what would be considered posterized color? Yes. You know, doing a lot of work with different codoliths so you can, you know, comp pictures inside of other pictures. Okay. So this turned out to be really fundamentally helpful a few years later. I went back, I saw my first hologram at a School of the Art Institute media and new technology show that was a number of grad students had put together. And believe it or not, there was a hologram in there from Dr. Jiang. Oh, what year was that? This was... It was like something like 76. And this is a hologram that was a little car. I think it was called Quick Turnaround. Okay. And it was a little circular hologram. Oh, that was one of his first 360 laser transmission cylinder holograms. Yeah. And I was very captured by that. At that point in my career, I was really kind of a fine art photographer. I had a 4x5 view camera. I used to spend my off days... Slept around Chicago doing black and white and color work. I had my own dye transfer lab in one of my bedrooms in my apartment. And I was doing color separations and doing... If your listeners are familiar with a photographer by the name of George Tice, it's kind of like urban landscape photography. Okay. And that's what I was doing in 75 and 74. And then I saw this hologram. And as an image maker in photography, I was very much about a printmaker. I really... Cared a lot about the quality of the print. That was a part of the process that communicated my vision or image through to the viewer. And I was very much an art photographer. And so I called my old instructor, Chuck Swedland, down at Southern Illinois. And I said, you know, I want to come back and finish up my senior year. And I've caught wind of this new thing called holography. And I want to know if you might let me spin that up into my... And I said, okay. And he said, okay. And I said, okay.

Zitter, who was over in the physics department. That's interesting. And Dr. Zitter had a helium neon laser. So they said, you know what, we can make this work. Come on back. So I went back down in 78, 77, 78 to finish my senior year and did kind of a mix of holography and photography. And I need to put something in here real important. After I saw my first hologram and found out that it was made by a physics professor up in Lake Forest, just north of Chicago, I went and signed up for his summer holography workshops. Oh, okay. And took two of them. And that really, it was like people were getting frustrated with me because all I ever talked about was holography and trying to get a laser. You were called to do this. It was just, yeah, it's like that little mouse or little squirrel that sees a shiny thing, needs to collect it. Something happened. I was just, I have to know how to do this. To me, it was an extension of the image. Now it was the ultimate printmaking. I wasn't dealing with dyes or silver anymore on a paper. I was able to make structures that diffracted light. So the color in my photographs could be light. That's what appealed to me. That's what got my dander up, as they say. And where did you go after that? Well, I came back and again, went back to work at the same company. They were actually kind of pleased that I came back in. I had a place called Gamma Photo and I had the job of the manager of the duplication department, which was like an extension of the stuff I'd been doing. But then I started pestering them. I started showing them my holograms that I was making. And I own a little five milliwatt laser. And at the time, when I moved back, I moved down into the western section of the Chicago Loop. That's where the old vegetable markets used to be near Fulton Street. I had a loft photography studio. I was still doing photography on the side, but I had to support myself. So I had a full-time job as the manager of this colored dupe department. And I'd bring them in my holograms and I'd show them and I'd say, you know, these are really, really getting kind of interesting to do. What do you think? And they kind of were like, you know, we're, we don't see this being interesting. Isn't that something? And they got, I got in trouble with the management. So I, at that point, was interested in doing holography full time and was trying to figure out a way to do it. And I was like, well, I'm going to do it. So I looked for another, another photo lab where they had an opening on the night shift so I could work from five in the evening until one in the morning. And then I had days to work in my little lab and took that job over at K&S Photographics. So now we're talking 79. And in the same time was, had built up my little lab, was doing holograms with a little 2.5 or 5 milliwatt Heaney. That was a major investment back then, a 5 milliwatt Heaney. That they were doing. Yeah. Yeah. That was like serious money. It was like more than $2,000. It certainly was. And, and it was like, and it was such a pitiful amount of light. And I was making little tiny, like one inch in diameter and reflection holograms that you could like barely see because nobody had really heard about pyrochrome yet. Okay. So we were doing all this, you know, really heavily silver laden holograms that were fixed. And because of the, you know, they shot in red, but there was all the silver in them and collapsing. And so they were green. You were probably working with, you know, with the mature chloride and some of those other chemicals. Yeah. Yeah. Good stuff. Bad news. And here's where the nice note, another little fun caveat happens. I'm going to have a lot of friends in my building that are students at the school of the art Institute. And I'm going to all the weekends, going to parties at different students' house. And I'm at a party one evening and I'm talking to a woman who's there, a girl, trying to make conversation. And at one point she just got frustrated and said, you know, there's another guy here who's trying to talk to me about the same stuff. This is holography stuff. I'm going to introduce you to him. You want to talk to somebody about this? Go talk to him. And she introduced me to Tom Svetkovich. Oh, yes. And so in meeting Tom, I found out there was somebody else that was like really keenly interested in holography and he was doing some consulting with Zenith. So that kind of spun. So in the summers, I'm doing like workshops and holography at Lake Forest. In the daytime, Tom and I are kind of talking about how can we make holograms work. Yeah. Yeah. And we started, we figured, well, one thing we can do is this is obviously more money than either one of us have. Why don't we try to do this thing? There was a young man, a guy in Chicago who had started a thing called a cooperative dark room where people could rent time on enlargers who didn't, you know, have a dark room. I thought, why couldn't we do something like that for holography? Why don't we have like a cooperative holography lab? And that began the Chicago Holographic Cooperative. Oh, I never, I have never heard of that. So connections, myself, Tom, some students, people, Victor Heredia, Rick Bruck, Melissa Crenshaw, a whole group of people that have been taking holography classes up at Lake Forest and also at the 1134 Gallery of Holography in Washington.

Rick Bruck, Melissa Crenshaw, a whole group of people that had been taking holography classes up at Lake Forest and also at the 1134 Gallery of Holography in Washington Street in Chicago, were all actually kind of milling around Chicago looking for, like, how can we do this? So we started meeting at my studio at 952 West Lake Street. It was a photography studio. And they had my little holography lab there that really wasn't much, but I was able to do some things. And we would have monthly meetings. What are you doing? Bring in holograms. Talk about holograms. Who wants to start a lab? You know, Tom had a laser, had some equipment. And we ended up meeting a woman that owned an old firehouse a couple blocks from me at 114 North Aberdeen. And she was like, I've got a tenant on the first floor. He's got a meatpacking company. Get these trucks with smelly meat in there. I'll be glad to rent you the first floor. Do whatever you want. So Tom and I took off. We got a lease. One-year lease. Took the back of it up to start with and built our first table. Wow. Started putting the table together. Now we're talking this late 79 and going into the spring of 1980. And we had the first table up. The darkroom processing was happening. And he and I had built, had been making, you know, he had a bigger laser. Yay. Red laser? Yep. And there we were. We were making four by five holograms. Yeah. I think that's right around the time of the first workshop, the symposium on holography. Okay. That would be 82. Okay. So right around 82, paper by Lon Moore. Color control. Oh, yes. And holography. Yes. Tom and I were like, oh, this is going to be hot. Right away, ran back to the lab. Started playing around with processing and the color control, which is P-benzoquinone, which is another really bad leach you didn't really want to be messing with. Anything comes in a package. It's a cardboard box. Inside of that is a aluminum foil cellophane bag that's been vacuum sealed, which inside of that is another glass container. Inside of that is another container. It's like in a skull and crossbones on the front. So P-benzoquinone from the holographer. That was to do your pseudo-color holograms, right? That's when we started doing pseudo-color holograms. And up at that point, we were meeting every day at the little holography lab in the back of this firehouse, making holograms, some single color, some transmission, trying to put together what would be the equivalent of a portfolio. I knew some art directors at a number of different agencies around Chicago. I had a couple of really good friends who were also photographers that were doing commercial photography work, and they were putting me in touch with people. And we put together three color control holograms and went into an advertising agency that was called Franklin Company. What holograms were they? And we met with a guy, an art director, whose name was Bill Takazuki. And at the time, he had a big client called McDonald's, and they were doing point-of-sale signage for McDonald's. He said, you know what? This is, like, really, really cool stuff. He said, if you had more equipment, could you make these bigger and could you do these better? Because he said, because nobody's ever come in here and showed me holograms that could be, this is that color and this is that color. So Tom and I came back. We set up their little exhibition room with the 12 different holograms. Two were laser-lit. A couple were, we even had built a case. The case was, like, took two people to carry it up, all made out of wood. All the little slots for the holograms were set in, the laser just set in. Wow. The whole thing. Set it up. They brought in a number of different account execs. It was there for about a four-hour period. We hung around and answered questions while people were there. Then a guy came there who was the account exec for McDonald's, and he said, we're going to have a meeting. Leave all this stuff here. I want you here tomorrow morning at 9 o'clock. Came in the next morning at 9, met the head buyer from the McDonald's Corporation. Spent all day at the agency talking about ideas. That was the day we called up Coherent and convinced them that they needed to sell us a 5-watt Krypton laser. Which was interesting. That's the whole story itself. It was self-convincing. Real-time, updatable 3D displays. I mean, if there was one thing that a hologram can do that. Other types of stereoscopic media cannot do. And that is a correctly rendered three-dimensional scene where convergence and focus are correct. I mean, our eyes are the most developed tool set of our whole body. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right.
